topics.topic: Atomic consistency of file name, metadata and bytes during concurrent replacement
questions: Must the name, metadata and bytes describe one atomic version of a file, and what happens if Syncthing-fork replaces the file while they are being read?
What consistency must hold between a file's name, metadata and bytes when Syncthing replaces or modifies it during a read?
Must the name, metadata and bytes describe one atomic snapshot, and how must the deliverer react if the file is replaced or modified between those reads?

quotes:
Syncthing may change the folder during a scan, so a scan is not a view of one instant. Each rule applies
to what its step finds when it runs, and the next scan sees the folder as it then stands.

One call delivers one photo, named by `name`, a relative path in the form a scan reports, and
   `source_id`. The service keeps no memory of earlier scans: it judges the name and the file when the call
   runs. The named file is read once, and the bytes that were read are the bytes judged, hashed and prepared.

Condition 1 is decided from the name and the metadata of its path before
   the file is opened, and conditions 2 to 4 from the opening on.
| 3 | the hash of the bytes differs from `source_id` | `SOURCE_CHANGED` |
judgement.why: State 2 permits a scan to observe different instants and defines delivery as one byte read whose actual bytes are judged, hashed and prepared, with changed content refused against the requested source id.

topics.topic: Metadata boundary schema and permitted influence on delivery decisions
questions: Which metadata fields cross this boundary, how are file types such as symlinks and special files represented, and which fields may influence eligibility, source identity, preparation or the publication body?
What information counts as file metadata at this boundary, including its fields, types, availability and distinction from metadata embedded in image bytes?
Which delivery decisions may depend on metadata, and which metadata fields, if any, contribute to source identity, eligibility, content-change detection or image preparation?
Which metadata fields and filesystem object types cross this boundary, in what representation, and which fields are required versus optional?

quotes: | Object folder → deliverer | file names, file metadata and bytes | untrusted, read only |
judgement.why: The exact metadata fields, filesystem representations, eligibility rules, identity inputs and preparation influences are rule and field-detail questions owned by State 2 rather than by State 0's requirement to name the boundary input.

topics.topic: Placement commit semantics and permitted side effects of failed delivery
questions: What precisely counts as a placement, and which writes or durable side effects are permitted when delivery fails?
What exact writes and state transition constitute a placement, and at what commit point may the deliverer report that placement succeeded?
Besides forbidding a placement, what state changes or writes are permitted on a failed delivery, including temporary files, rejection records, caches, counters and changes to an earlier placement?
What constitutes a placement, and which writes or stored facts, if any, are permitted when delivery fails?

quotes:
The record that one source photo of one project was placed in the Portal binary store. The
deliverer creates it once when placing a photo.

Conditions 1 to 4 write nothing except the
   project lock. After condition 5 a stored image may remain without a record: no caller has received
   its reference, and a repeated delivery of the same file writes it again and completes the placement.

The stored image is written before the placement record, so a crash between them repeats the
   placement and leaves no record without an image.
A replaced source is a new photo. The earlier placement, its stored image and its mark stay.
judgement.why: States 1 and 2 define the placement record, the write order, the permitted project-lock side effect for early failures, the possible orphan image after a record-write failure and preservation of earlier placements.

topics.topic: Source ID and result schema for rejected files
questions: Does a rejected file also carry its source id, or is the source id present only for ready, placed and published files?
Does a rejected file also carry its source id, and is rejected itself a status or a separate result shape?
Is rejected a status, and exactly which result variants include a source id and a reason so every returned file can be correlated with a later delivery request?

quotes:
`source_id` is present for `ready`, `placed` and
`published` and absent for `rejected`, `reason` is present only for `rejected`, `file_ref` for `placed`
and `published`, and `photo_id` only for `published`.

**Fields:** `name: str` (the path relative to the photo folder, with `/` separators), `size: int`,
`source_id: str | None`, `status: ScanStatus`, `reason: ObservationReason | None`,
`file_ref: str | None`, `photo_id: UUID | None`.
judgement.why: State 1 explicitly makes rejected a status, omits source_id from rejected observations and limits reason to rejected observations.

topics.topic: Handling and reporting invalid, unreadable, unsupported or changing metadata
questions: What happens when metadata is unreadable, unsupported, malformed or changes during inspection: is that file rejected, is the whole project request refused, or is the metadata ignored?
What must the deliverer do, and what observable reason must it return, when metadata is malformed, unreadable, unsupported or changes during inspection?

quotes: | Object folder → deliverer | file names, file metadata and bytes | untrusted, read only |
judgement.why: The classification and ordering of malformed, unreadable, unsupported or concurrently changing metadata are operational rules owned by State 2, not an unnamed State 0 actor, input, output, fact, system, boundary or promise.

topics.topic: Policy for links and other non-regular filesystem objects, including traversal outside the root
questions: Are symbolic links, hard links, devices, sockets and other non-regular objects permitted, and may metadata or byte reads follow a link outside the connected root?

quotes: A scan gives each regular file of the photo folder exactly one status.

Ignored names are not reported, ignored folders are not entered,
and an entry the listing shows as a symbolic link is neither reported nor followed.
| 3 | opened in non-blocking mode without following a link, what it finds is not a regular file | `rejected` | `not_a_regular_file` |
| 5 | opening or reading it fails, which includes a file that disappeared and a path that became a symbolic link after the listing | `rejected` | `unreadable_file` |

| 1 | `name` is not non-empty segments joined by single `/` characters, or a segment is `.` or `..`, or a segment is ignored under A1, or a folder on its path is absent or a symbolic link, or the last segment is absent or is not a regular file, or the metadata of a segment cannot be read. Names are compared exactly, without Unicode normalisation | `NOT_READY_OR_ABSENT` |
judgement.why: State 2 admits regular files, rejects other opened objects, and requires symbolic links at listing time, along the requested path or appearing before opening to be omitted or refused without being followed.
